title: FRM Operational, Lesson 8: People risk - key staff, incentives and a speak-up culture
subtitle: A process is only as good as what people do when nobody is watching
whyItMatters: All seven Basel event categories have a person somewhere in the causal chain. Yet people risk rarely gets a line of its own in a risk report, because it is hard to measure and hard to talk about - and that is exactly why it is the least well managed part of the whole operational risk framework.
openingQuestion: A trading desk has produced excellent results for years, is run by one person, and that person has never taken an extended holiday. What is this a sign of?
openingOptions: A dedicated employee the organisation should retain at almost any cost
A warning worth checking, because never taking leave is a signal
A pure human resources matter that falls outside the risk framework
A sign that the handover procedure for the desk is working properly
explanation: This is why mandatory block leave persists at financial institutions and is treated as a control rather than a benefit: concealment has to be maintained daily, so two weeks of enforced absence is the window in which it is most likely to surface. At the same time, one person holding all the knowledge of a profitable activity is key-person risk - the organisation loses the capability the moment that person leaves, for whatever reason.

diagram.label: Key-person risk: one person holds knowledge nobody can replace
Incentives: bonuses tied to short-term results pull behaviour with them
Speak-up culture: can someone who sees a problem actually say so
Controls: mandatory leave, job rotation, anonymous reporting channels

realWorldExample.description: The pattern repeats to a striking degree: the person responsible is usually a highly regarded employee who works very long hours, rarely takes leave, and previously worked in the back office and so knows exactly what each control looks at. None of those facts is evidence on its own, but the cluster appearing together is what a good risk framework has to notice.

quiz.question: Why is mandatory block leave treated as an operational risk control?
options: Because it lowers staff costs during the quieter part of the year
Because a well-rested employee makes fewer operational mistakes
Because employment law requires a minimum number of days off each year
Because concealment has to be maintained daily and surfaces during an absence
quiz.explanation: Most fraud has to be covered up continuously - rolling positions forward, adjusting entries, intercepting confirmations. Two consecutive weeks of absence is the window in which a stand-in sees things that have never been looked at before. Employee wellbeing is a genuine benefit but not the reason the rule sits in the control framework, and the statutory leave entitlement says nothing about taking it in an unbroken block, which is the part that does the work.

quiz.question: Which sign most clearly indicates key-person risk?
options: One activity that only a single person understands well enough to run
Attrition across the whole department rising over the course of the year
The department's payroll cost running ahead of the approved budget
The number of staff holding a professional qualification being low
quiz.explanation: When only one person understands a model, a process or a system, the organisation loses the capability the instant they leave - and it also loses any way of checking their work while they stay. The two exposures travel together and both are treated with rotation and documentation. Rising attrition and a payroll overrun are management problems of a different kind, and a shortage of qualifications is about depth of skill across a team rather than dependence on one individual.

quiz.question: How does a bonus scheme tied to short-term results create operational risk?
options: It pushes staff costs beyond a level the business can sustain
It rewards tail risk, because the consequences arrive later
It causes the strongest employees to leave for better-paying firms
It affects only the front office and never the operations function
quiz.explanation: A strategy that takes on rare but severe risk delivers steady profit for several periods before the tail arrives. If the bonus is paid period by period and never clawed back, the risk-taker has been paid in full long before the loss shows up. This is why deferral and clawback became regulatory requirements after 2008. Pay levels and staff turnover are real management issues, but they do not distort the risk being taken, which is the mechanism at work here.

quiz.question: What indicates that an organisation's speak-up culture is not working?
options: The compliance function receives a lot of questions from employees
The number of internally reported incidents rises year after year
After an incident, several people say they saw it and did not report it
Employees regularly put forward suggestions for improving processes
quiz.explanation: The worrying finding is not that nobody spotted the problem but that several people spotted it and none of them spoke. The other three are all signs of health rather than sickness: a rising count of internal reports usually means people believe reporting will not be held against them, and questions to compliance mean the rules are being engaged with rather than quietly worked around. Reading a rising report count as deterioration is the classic misinterpretation here.

quiz.question: Why is job rotation both a fraud control and a control on key-person risk?
options: Because it is a licensing condition for operating in the industry
Because it reduces the long-run cost of training new employees
Because it gives employees an additional reason to stay with the firm
Because knowledge has to be shared and the old work gets fresh eyes
quiz.explanation: A seat that never changes hands is a seat nobody else understands and nobody else can check. Rotation solves both at once: the knowledge has to be written down and handed over, and the previous work is exposed to a new pair of eyes. Retention and training costs move in either direction depending on the design, and no regulator makes rotation a condition of licensing - it is a control firms adopt because it addresses two exposures with one measure.

practicePrompt.question: One specialist is the only person who understands and runs the pricing model for a product line, and for four years has never taken more than two consecutive days off. How many risks is this?
options: Two: the capability is lost if they leave, and nobody can check the work
One: key-person risk, addressed through a succession plan
One: fraud risk, addressed through a mandatory leave policy
None at all, since deep expertise is an asset for the organisation
practicePrompt.explanation: Two different risks are stacked on the same person. The first is capability: if they resign, the organisation loses the ability to price a product line and nobody understands it well enough to take over. The second is control: if nobody else can run the model, nobody can verify its output, and an error - deliberate or not - can persist for years. Four years without a break is the classic signal, because a layer of concealment needs daily maintenance. Job rotation addresses both at once, which is why it is classified as a control rather than as an HR policy.

keyTakeaways: Mandatory leave is a fraud control, not a benefit - concealment needs daily maintenance and surfaces during an absence
One person understanding an activity is two risks at once: lost capability when they go, and no verification while they stay
Short-term bonuses reward taking tail risk, because the consequence arrives after the payout period
The sign of a broken culture is not that nobody saw the problem but that several people saw it and none spoke

summary.keyIdea: A procedure covers the part of the job that can be written as a procedure. The rest - what people do when nobody is watching - is decided by incentives and culture, and that is where the most severe operational losses usually begin.

application.message: For each important activity you are responsible for, ask who would cover it if the person doing it were away for two weeks. No clear answer means you have found a risk, and usually two.

sections.text: All seven Basel event categories have a person in the causal chain. Yet people risk rarely gets a line of its own in a risk report - hard to measure, and hard to say out loud.

At many financial institutions two consecutive weeks of leave is mandatory and is checked. The reason has nothing to do with employee wellbeing: concealment has to be maintained daily, and two weeks of absence is the window in which a stand-in sees things nobody has ever looked at. A person who never takes leave is therefore a fact worth noticing, even though on its own it proves nothing.
When only one person understands it

A pricing model only its author understands, a reconciliation only one person can run - that is both the risk of losing the capability when they leave and the risk of nobody being able to check the work while they stay. Two sides of one problem, with one remedy: documentation and rotation.
Incentives pull behaviour harder than rules do

If bonuses are paid on annual results and never clawed back, taking on rare but severe risk is the individually optimal strategy: several years of steady profit, the bonus already banked, and when the tail arrives the loss belongs to the firm. No rulebook can stand against a pay structure pushing the other way.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: A rising number of internally reported incidents is usually good news rather than bad: it says people believe that speaking up will not be held against them.
